back: Service level indicator: a quantitative measure of service, best written as good events / valid events.
Service level objective: a target for an SLI over a window, e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed over a rolling 28 days.
A contract with consequences (credits, termination) if missed. No consequence means it is an SLO. Set looser than the internal SLO.
4.32 minutes. Each extra nine divides the budget by ten.
Users cannot see past their own networks' unreliability, and 100% leaves zero budget for any change.

front: Why is CPU usage not an SLI?
back: Users do not experience CPU; they experience failed or slow requests. CPU is a cause signal for capacity and debugging.
Fraction of valid requests faster than a threshold (e.g. 300 ms), from a histogram with a bucket boundary at that threshold.
0.999³ ≈ 99.7% is the best you can offer without retries, caching or redundancy.
Observed error rate / (1 − SLO). Burn rate 1 spends exactly the whole budget over the window.
Burn rate × duration / SLO window. 14.4 × 1 h / 720 h = 2%.
14.4× over 1 h (5 min short window) = 2% of budget; 6× over 6 h (30 min) = 5%. Ticket: 1× over 3 days (6 h) = 10%.
Reset time: the alert clears minutes after recovery instead of waiting for the 1-hour average to fall.
14.4 × 0.1% = 1.44% error rate over both 1 hour and 5 minutes.
Rolling: no reset cliff, same weekday mix, matches user memory. Calendar: simpler for business reporting and SLAs.
Pre-agreed rules for when the budget is spent, e.g. freeze non-urgent releases, postmortem any incident over 20% of budget, named escalation.
The SLO is too loose to matter or the team is too cautious: ship faster, run experiments, or tighten the target.
